### Observed differences

- In the later window, the elapsed time between consecutive completions of A14 and A26 is roughly twice as long as before: about 1.9 hours on average (median about 1.9 hours, 101 intervals) versus about 1.0 hour in the earlier window (median about 1.0 hour, 93 intervals) — an increase of about 0.9 hours. [TWAIT001]
- The pair A18–A26 shows the same shift: intervals averaged about 1.0 hour before (107 intervals) and about 2.0 hours in the later window (99 intervals) — an increase of about 1.0 hour. [TWAIT002]
- In both pairs the whole distribution moved upward: the middle 50% of intervals rose from roughly 0.9–1.1 hours to roughly 1.8–2.3 hours, and the spread roughly doubled (standard deviation from about 0.15 to about 0.3 hours), so intervals became both longer and more variable. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]
- How often each consecutive pair occurs stayed similar (93 vs 101 intervals for A14–A26; 107 vs 99 for A18–A26), so the difference lies in duration, not in how often the pairs occur. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]
- Both differences are larger than those seen in all but about 1 of 2000 random re-splits of the two windows. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a timing hypothesis: in the later window, the elapsed time between consecutive completion events involving A26 is about twice as long as before — from about 1 hour to about 2 hours — on both the A14–A26 and the A18–A26 transitions. Supporting signs: two time items with the same direction and similar magnitude (about 0.9 and 1.0 hours), each based on substantial observation counts (93–107 intervals per window) and each more extreme than all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits; the time family produced 2 qualifying items where about 0.008 were expected if nothing had changed (16 units tested), a count far beyond chance, while no control-flow items qualified (0 against about 0.29 expected). The stable pair counts indicate a change in duration rather than in participation or routing. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Limitations: TWAIT measures elapsed time between consecutive completions, so the evidence does not show whether the extra hour is waiting, processing or intervening work between the two events. Both flagged pairs share A26, so the two items may reflect one underlying behaviour rather than two independent changes; and only these two of 16 time units qualified, which points to the intervals around A26 specifically rather than a uniform slowdown, but the evidence cannot rule out timing effects outside the tested units. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]

Other differences: none — the only qualified evidence items are the two timing items above. [TWAIT001, TWAIT002]
